A1.justification: Both 16-page PDFs describe the same Ubuntu-CG study. Their main texts, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support matching of retained, revised and relocated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotations of 200 conversations, grounding-act analysis of 70 conversations, encoder and LLM evaluations, and human assessment of model explanations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical investigations, revises dataset statistics and detection results, and reports an additional aggregation of model scores in Table 11.

M1.justification: The per-turn distilroberta classifier and whole-conversation LLM prompting, with or without technical elaborations, remain unchanged. Section 5.1's added single-pass explanation documents the existing procedure rather than introducing a new component.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 200 Ubuntu conversations, 70-conversation grounding subset and 64-instance explanation assessment, covering the same detection, success-prediction and explanation tasks. Revised annotation counts do not establish different task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8b/70b-Instruct, their elaboration variants, and distilroberta with context windows of three and five. Table 11 reuses the existing detection comparator set.

E3.justification: The principal detection evaluation expands from one summary to separate aggregations giving equal weight to conversations in Table 6 and friction instances in Table 11. Sections 5.2–6 also change the stated error-analysis configuration from GPT-4o with elaborations to plain GPT-4o. The unchanged error-analysis numbers do not establish that those analyses were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix A.8/Table 11 adds an alternative aggregation, and Section 5.2 examines baseline competitiveness under that weighting. This supplements the analysis of sensitivity to aggregation. The binary-friction and success ablations, conversational-depth and repair analyses, and explanation case studies remain.

E5.justification: The five random splits, inter-rater agreement measures, standard-deviation reporting and Section 6 significance tests remain unchanged. Revised standard deviations and additional aggregate scores do not introduce new uncertainty-reporting practices or documented additional runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes conversations containing friction from 122 to 109, and the reported gold interval total changes from 266 to 238. Detection scores are extensively revised: GPT-4o's Found/Overlap F1 values are 51.36/21.77 in v1 Table 6, versus 34.01/14.61 and 46.38/19.29 in v2 Tables 6 and 11. Plain GPT-4o replaces its elaboration variant as the overlap-F1 leader. These revised references and aggregations prevent interpreting the differences as same-setting performance losses.

T1.justification: The friction-interval definitions, overlap criteria, Jaccard matching and asymmetric agreement construction in Section 3.2 remain unchanged. The additional empirical aggregation descriptions introduce no substantive formal derivation, theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central claims: friction reflects common-ground misalignment and relates to task success, while LLMs struggle with implicit cases. The claimed contribution concerning naturally occurring, text-only task-oriented dialogue is unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 now qualifies the apparent competitiveness of encoder baselines by the aggregation used, emphasizing equal weighting of friction instances. The observer-versus-participant limitation is retained from v1 Appendix A.7 and moved into the main Limitations section, rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 explicitly documents that decoder models predict all friction intervals in one pass, clarifying their implementation distinction from per-turn encoder predictions. Hyperparameters, hardware, quantization, prompts and code/data access information remain unchanged. The added main-text annotation-allocation statement was already documented in v1 Appendix A.1.

R1.justification: v2 adds Shaikh et al. (2025) on human–LLM grounding, İnan et al. (2025) on positive friction, and Hu and Frank (2024) on auxiliary task demands. These additions modestly expand positioning and distinguish the paper's friction concept from beneficial conversational friction.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized language corrections and explanatory edits, updates an author name, adds acknowledgments, and moves the metalinguistic-capability discussion from the appendix to Limitations. The overall narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 11, enlarges Table 6 and expands its caption to explain aggregation. Table 8 moves to the next page and the appendix layout reflows. Figures 1–4 retain their visual content.

improvement.justification: The additional aggregation results and clearer research positioning are useful, but the empirical revisions have unresolved reporting problems. v1's overall and successful-conversation friction rates, 61% and 53.33%, agree with Table 2. v2's prose reports 61% and 54.5%, while its revised table implies 54.5% overall and reports 50.84% for successful conversations. The unexplained change from 266 to 238 gold intervals and reassignment of unchanged error-analysis statistics also obscure whether the revision corrects underlying errors. These benefits and uncertainties prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
